name: Febrile Neutropenia

likely: Coagulase-negative staphylococci (especially if central line present)
possible: Candida species and other fungi if fever persists beyond 4-7 days on antibacterial therapy
pathogens.why: Antipseudomonal coverage is mandatory by definition in febrile neutropenia given the rapid, often source-occult progression Pseudomonas bacteremia can cause in neutropenic hosts. Gram-positive organisms become more relevant with central lines or severe mucositis; fungal coverage is escalated only if fever is persistent despite adequate antibacterial therapy.

investigations.test: Blood cultures (peripheral and from each lumen of central line if present)
investigations.why: Identifies bacteremia and distinguishes line-associated infection, both common and consequential in this population.
Tracks neutrophil recovery, which determines duration of antibiotics and risk stratification.
Screens for pulmonary source even when respiratory symptoms are minimal, since neutropenic patients may lack typical localizing signs.
Screens for urinary source even in the absence of typical symptoms.
Stratifies low- versus high-risk febrile neutropenia, which determines candidacy for oral/outpatient therapy versus mandatory inpatient IV therapy.

references: NCCN Guidelines for Prevention and Treatment of Cancer-Related Infections
reasonSource: ()=>"Fever (single temperature ≥38.3°C or ≥38.0°C sustained for 1 hour) in a patient with neutropenia (ANC <500/µL or expected to fall below 500) is a medical emergency by definition. Empiric broad-spectrum antipseudomonal antibiotics must be administered within 1 hour of presentation without waiting for culture results, since this population can progress rapidly to severe sepsis with minimal localizing signs."
